newsitem.title: TURKEY: Pressures mount on deficit-ridden Turkish economy.
newsitem.headline: Pressures mount on deficit-ridden Turkish economy.

text.p: Turkey's economy has come under increasing pressure from high inflation and big deficits but analysts on Tuesday saw no signs of near-term action, which they say is needed to ward off a downward spiral.
"A crisis is on the way, the government sleeps," liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil headlined on Tuesday.

Izzettin Onder, an economics professor at the Istanbul University, said that signals from the overall economy pointed to a crisis. "But a crisis is unlikely in the short term unless inflow of foreign funds stops," he told Reuters.
Husammetin Kavi, head of Istanbul Chamber of Industry, said no imminent action by the government was seen on the horizon.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's resource plan, unveiled in July, has failed to fuel optimism among economists who think the plan is unrealistic and unapplicable. Erbakan expects his plan to raise $10 billion in the next three years.
But economists say this target is unlikely to be reached, urging a medium-term stability programme.

Bankers say short-term capital inflow, propelled by high real domestic interest rates, strong foreign reserves at around $16 billion, and decisive actions by the central bank and treasury may prevent a near-term financial crisis.
But they note that increased concerns over the economy have been pushing up Turkey's risk premium in foreign debt markets.
"Most of the mandates given earlier this year for foreign loans arrangements have been shelved. The costs have risen," said a senior private banker.

"A medium-scale Turkish bank can not get a syndicated loan at prices lower than Libor (London Interbank Offered Rate) plus 150 basis points now. It was around 110-120 basis point over Libor in June," said the banker, who declined to be named.
After months of political turmoil and delay in key economic actions, almost all economists and officials agreed that Turkey would fail to achieve this year's economic targets.
In early 1996, the government set the year-on-year inflation target at 65 percent. Economists forecast inflation, 79 percent last month, will probably stand at above 80 percent at end-1996.
The current account deficit may overshoot the target -- $3.8 billion -- by some $1 billion and foreign trade deficit may exceed $20 billion against the target of $16 billion.
The official 861-trillion lira ($9.7 billion) budget deficit target has meant nothing for economists since Finance Minister Abdullatif Sener said in July the deficit could hit 1,300 trillion lira.
Turkey's military build-up in the southeast against rebel Kurds and delays in Iraqi oil-for-food plan, which was hoped to earn Ankara over $500 million, also worsened fiscal pains.
Faruk Selcuk, an associate professor of economics, said the public sector borrowing requirement may rise to 14 percent of gross national product (GNP) from about six percent last year.

GNP growth rate, 10.3 percent in the first half of the year, is expected to remain well above the target of 4.5 percent -- seen as another sign of instability and the economy's inability to achieve sustainable and moderate economic growth.
Privatisation efforts have almost come to a standstill. Turkey has raised $292 million through sell-offs so far this year, far below the 1996 target of $2 billion.
Any new attempts to increase privatisation earnings are not expected to bring an additional amount of more than $500 million in the rest of this year.
The absence of firm economic action to increase government revenues soon leaves borrowing as the major but costly source of funds to finance public deficits.
The treasury pays an annual compound rate of around 120 percent to borrow from domestic markets.
The government's plan to issue foreign currency denominated bonds with a maturity of up to three years to ease pressures were seen raising only some $1 billion.
Bankers say concerns about the economy and a sub-investment grade credit rating, were also restraining Turkey's ability to raise funds in international markets at "reasonable" rates.
The treasury, which last issued 500 million marks of Eurobonds with a coupon of 8.5 percent in July, has delayed a Samurai bond issue, initially planned for July.
